Physi- cal incompatibilities due to the low pH of metronidazole injec- tions appear to be more of a problem than chemical incompati- bility. Regardless of these studies, it is generally recommended that other drugs should not be added to intravenous solutions of metronidazole or its hydrochloride. Adverse Effects The adverse effects of metronidazole are generally dose-related. The most common are gastrointestinal disturbances, especially nausea and an unpleasant metallic taste. Vomiting, and diarrhoea or constipation may also occur. A furred tongue, glossitis, and stoma- titis may be associated with an overgrowth of Candida. There have been rare reports of antibiotic-associated colitis associated with metronidazole, although it is also used in the treatment of this condition. Weakness, dizziness, ataxia, headache, drowsiness, in- somnia, and changes in mood or mental state such as depression or confusion have also been reported. Pe- ripheral neuropathy, usually presenting as numbness or tingling in the extremities, and epileptiform seizures have been associated with high doses of metronidazole or prolonged treatment.
